content.title: Christianity & Islam
content.subtitle: Explore the essential differences.
content.description: Who is God? Who is Jesus? How are we forgiven? Explore twelve questions about the Christian truth and Islamic perspective, with Scripture and the relevant Qur’anic passages beside each answer.

christian.text:
Jesus is the eternal Son who became truly human: one person, fully God and fully man. John identifies the Word as God before speaking of the Word becoming flesh.

Christ’s humanity does not replace his deity. The Christian confession concerns the identity of the person who came to save us, not simply his place among religious teachers.

other.text:
Qur’an 4:171 calls Jesus Messiah and messenger, a word communicated to Mary and a spirit from God. The same passage rejects divine sonship and tells its hearers not to say three.

These titles must be read within that rejection. They should not be turned into an admission that the Qur’an teaches the Christian incarnation.

christian.text:
There is one divine being in three distinct persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Scripture affirms God’s unity while naming the Father, Son and Spirit together.

This is neither three gods nor one person changing roles. The distinction is between who the persons are and the one divine being they share.

other.text:
Qur’an 112 affirms God’s oneness, denies begetting and being begotten, and declares that none is comparable to him. Qur’an 4:171 rejects the language of three.

The agreement that God is one does not settle the disagreement about the Trinity. The comparison must address what each text says about that oneness.

christian.text:
Christ died for our sins, was buried and rose bodily. His death is a willing saving act, and his resurrection belongs to the gospel Paul proclaims.

The cross is therefore more than the death of a prophet. Removing Christ’s death for sin removes the atoning work central to the Christian message.

other.text:
Qur’an 4:157 denies that Jesus’ opponents killed or crucified him; 4:158 says that God raised him. The text does not name a person substituted for Jesus.

Keep the passage’s wording separate from later explanations of what happened. Ask which interpretation your neighbour holds before responding to it.

rows.question: What does Son of God mean?

christian.text:
The Son’s relation to the Father is eternal. The Christian confession does not describe God producing a child through a sexual act.

The Son already is before creation; the incarnation is his taking human nature. Explaining that distinction addresses a misunderstanding without removing the real disagreement.

other.text:
Qur’an 112:3 denies that God begets or is begotten, and 4:171 rejects God’s having a son. These statements set a boundary for the passage’s description of Jesus.

Clarifying that Christians do not mean biological procreation does not make the Qur’anic rejection disappear. The eternal sonship Christians confess remains the point to examine.

christian.text:
The Word exists before creation, and everything that was made came into being through him. The Son is not included among the creatures he made.

His human nature belongs to the incarnation; it does not mean that the eternal Son began to exist when Jesus was born.

other.text:
Qur’an 3:59 compares Jesus with Adam in relation to God’s creative command. The verse points to God’s power to bring into being.

Read this comparison beside 4:171 rather than treating Jesus’ extraordinary origin as a confession of his eternal deity.

rows.question: What is our problem with sin?

christian.text:
All have sinned and fall short of God’s glory. Romans also connects the human condition with Adam’s disobedience and contrasts it with Christ’s obedience.

The Christian answer addresses both our own sins and our need for the righteousness and life Christ gives.

other.text:
Qur’an 53:38–42 stresses that a burdened soul does not bear another’s burden and that each person’s endeavour receives recompense.

These verses foreground personal responsibility. They should be examined alongside the Christian account of Adam and Christ, without claiming that this brief passage surveys every Islamic discussion of human nature.

christian.text:
Forgiveness is received through Christ’s blood, according to the riches of God’s grace. God’s mercy is joined to Christ’s saving work.

The Christian proclamation explains forgiveness through the one who bears our sins, not by treating the cross as unnecessary.

other.text:
Qur’an 39:53 calls sinners not to despair of God’s mercy. The following verse calls them to turn back and submit to God.

Islamic forgiveness must not be portrayed as mercyless. The comparison concerns the grounds and means of forgiveness, especially the place of Christ’s atoning work.

christian.text:
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works as grounds for boasting. Good works follow: believers are created in Christ for a life of obedience.

The gift and its fruit must be kept together. Christian obedience does not purchase the salvation Christ gives.

other.text:
Qur’an 53:39–41 describes human endeavour and recompense, while 39:53–54 speaks of mercy, repentance and submission.

Read both themes together. The slogan that Muslims simply earn salvation leaves out the mercy these texts affirm; the disagreement still includes the saving work and identity of Christ.

christian.text:
God spoke through the prophets and has spoken in his Son. Hebrews presents the Son as the radiance of God’s glory, not merely another messenger in a sequence.

Christian revelation centres on the Son’s identity and work, with Scripture providing the authoritative testimony we examine.

other.text:
Qur’an 4:163 places revelation to Muhammad alongside revelation to earlier prophets, naming figures including Abraham, Moses’ family and Jesus. Verses 164–165 describe messengers bringing good news and warnings.

This presents a claimed continuity of prophetic revelation. The Christian comparison asks whether that claim agrees with what the earlier Scriptures teach about the Son.

christian.text:
A later message must be tested against the gospel already proclaimed. Galatians warns against a different gospel even if its messenger claims heavenly authority.

The Christian assessment therefore begins with the message’s agreement with Christ and his gospel, rather than accepting a prophetic title as its own proof.

other.text:
Qur’an 33:40 describes Muhammad as God’s messenger and the seal of the prophets. Qur’an 4:163 places his revelation in continuity with earlier prophets.

These passages establish the Qur’an’s claim about Muhammad. Testing that claim requires examining the message and its grounds, not treating the assertion itself as independent verification.

christian.text:
Scripture is God-breathed and equips the believer. In this library it is the final authority against which teaching is measured.

A later religious text is not accepted as a correction of the apostolic gospel merely because it claims to confirm earlier revelation.

other.text:
Qur’an 5:48 describes the Book revealed to Muhammad as confirming earlier Scripture and having authority over it in the linked translation. It calls for judgment by what God revealed.

The point to examine is how the Qur’an’s claimed relationship to earlier Scripture fits their actual contents. This verse alone does not settle every question about biblical manuscripts or interpretation.

christian.text:
The Westminster Confession teaches that God has preserved Scripture through his care and providence. Christians can examine the manuscript witnesses while confessing that preservation.

Distinguish the doctrinal claim from the historical questions about particular copies, variants and translations; a short comparison cannot replace that examination.

other.text:
Qur’an 15:9 promises that God will preserve the Reminder. The linked context identifies the Reminder with the revelation being challenged by Muhammad’s opponents.

A promise of preservation is a claim to examine. It is not itself a complete historical account of the transmission of either the Qur’an or the Bible.

readingPlan.introduction: These readings serve a Christian conversation about trusting Jesus: understand God’s identity, examine Jesus’ identity, consider forgiveness through his death and resurrection, then assess the claims of revelation. Read each Qur’anic passage on its own terms beside the Christian counterpart. Ask what your neighbour believes and why; the sequence guides discussion rather than guaranteeing conversion.

stages.title: Who is God?
stages.aim: Establish what each person means by one God before discussing Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

readings.title: One God: the shared starting point

context.text: Read the complete four-verse chapter. It confesses God’s oneness, rejects begetting and being begotten, and denies any equal to him.

purpose.text: Understand why divine sonship can sound like a denial of God’s uniqueness to a Muslim neighbour.

examine.text: Read all four verses together. Distinguish the rejection of begetting from the Christian meaning of the eternal Son; ask what your neighbour thinks Christians mean.

connection.text: Begin with the objection the person actually holds. Shared monotheistic language opens the discussion but does not settle the disagreement about God.

christian.text: Christian Scripture also confesses one God. Jesus commands baptism in the singular name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit; the comparison concerns how this confession fits together, rather than whether Christians worship three gods.

stages.title: Who is Jesus?
stages.aim: Move from shared names for Jesus to the decisive difference about his identity.

context.text: The passage addresses the People of the Book. It calls Jesus Messiah and messenger, speaks of God’s word and a spirit from him, and rejects saying three and attributing a son to God.

purpose.text: Identify both the honour given to Jesus and the boundaries placed around that honour.

examine.text: Read the whole address. Keep the descriptions of Jesus beside the explicit qualifications. Ask how your neighbour interprets word, spirit and sonship.

connection.text: This explains why agreement that Jesus is Messiah is not yet agreement with the gospel. The next question is what makes him more than a messenger.

christian.text: John identifies the Word as God and says the Word became flesh. Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as Lord and God. These passages explain the Christian claim without importing it into the Qur’an’s wording.

readings.title: Jesus and Adam: what creation proves

context.text: In the surrounding discussion of Jesus, this verse compares him to Adam: God created Adam from dust and brought him into being by command.

purpose.text: Examine the argument that Jesus’ extraordinary origin does not itself establish divinity.

examine.text: Follow the comparison with Adam. Identify what the verse explains about creation and what it does not establish about the Christian claim of incarnation.

connection.text: A Christian answer should explain Jesus’ identity from the biblical testimony, rather than argue that a virgin birth alone proves he is God.

christian.text: John places the Word before creation and attributes creation to him, then describes his becoming flesh. The Christian distinction is between the Creator taking human nature and a creature receiving an extraordinary beginning.

stages.title: How are we forgiven?
stages.aim: Bring the discussion to sin, mercy and the saving work Christians proclaim at the cross.

context.text: Read verses 157–158 together. The passage denies that Jesus’ opponents killed or crucified him and says God raised him to himself.

purpose.text: Locate the disagreement that directly concerns the Christian account of salvation.

examine.text: Separate the words of the passage from a translator’s additions and later explanations. The verses do not name a substitute; ask which interpretation your neighbour follows.

connection.text: Conversion to Christianity involves trusting the crucified and risen Jesus. Explain why his death belongs to the gospel before discussing alternative accounts.

christian.text: Paul’s summary places Christ’s death for sins, burial, resurrection and witnesses at the centre of the received gospel. This is the claim the Qur’anic account must be compared with.

readings.title: Mercy, repentance and the ground of forgiveness

context.text: Verse 53 offers hope to people who have sinned. Continue through 54–55, which call them to return, submit and follow revelation before judgment.

purpose.text: Hear the promise of mercy accurately before explaining the Christian account of grace.

examine.text: Read the invitation and the response together. Ask what your neighbour understands to be the ground of forgiveness, rather than assuming Islam has no mercy.

connection.text: The conversation can now ask how forgiveness is received and why Christians connect it to Christ’s saving work.

christian.text: Ephesians describes salvation by grace through faith as God’s gift, followed by a life of good works. Romans connects justification to redemption in Christ, explaining the ground of Christian assurance.

context.text: Verse 38 concerns the punishment of theft. Verse 39 immediately speaks of repentance, reform and God’s forgiveness. Read both.

purpose.text: Distinguish legal consequences, moral guilt and forgiveness instead of treating a penalty as a complete account of salvation.

examine.text: Notice the legal setting and the following invitation to repent. Ask how your neighbour understands its application; this reading does not establish every Muslim’s legal position.

connection.text: The passage helps clarify the problem the gospel addresses: wrongdoing requires more than a comparison of punishments. Ask how guilt before God is answered.

christian.text: Romans explains that the law exposes sin and that justification is given through Christ. This is a comparison about guilt and redemption, rather than a matching Christian civil penalty for theft.

stages.title: Which revelation should we trust?
stages.aim: Identify the competing claims of authority, then distinguish those claims from the evidence needed to assess them.

readings.title: A claim of continuity with earlier prophets

context.text: Read 163–166. Muhammad’s revelation is placed alongside earlier prophets, including Jesus; the surrounding verses describe messengers bringing good news and warning.

purpose.text: Understand why a Muslim may see Islam as continuation rather than a departure from earlier revelation.

examine.text: Identify the named prophets and the continuity being claimed. Ask whether shared names also mean agreement about their message.

connection.text: After discussing Jesus and the cross, ask whether the later message preserves or changes the earlier one. A list of prophets does not itself resolve that question.

christian.text: Hebrews describes God’s earlier speech through prophets and his climactic speech in the Son, who reveals God and makes purification for sins. Christian continuity centres on the identity and work of Jesus.

context.text: Read 37–40. The discussion includes adoption and marriage before identifying Muhammad as God’s messenger and the seal of the prophets.

purpose.text: Identify the basis for the claim that Muhammad’s message has final prophetic authority.

examine.text: Keep the statement in its surrounding argument. Ask what seal of the prophets means to your neighbour and how that authority is assessed.

connection.text: The disagreement now concerns which message can govern the understanding of Jesus. Naming a final messenger states a claim; it does not independently prove it.

christian.text: Paul tells Christians to test even a later messenger against the gospel already received. This explains the Christian criterion for accepting a message, while leaving the truth of the competing claims open to examination.

context.text: The chapter discusses Torah and Gospel before describing the Qur’an as confirming earlier Scripture and having authority over it; verses 49–50 continue the theme of judgment.

purpose.text: Expose the question of which text governs interpretation when their accounts differ.

examine.text: Compare translations of the authority language. Identify what the passage says about confirmation and judgment, and distinguish this from a demonstrated history of textual corruption.

connection.text: This directs the discussion to actual texts and evidence. Do not use this verse alone either to prove the Bible is corrupted or to assume it settles every disagreement in Christianity’s favour.

christian.text: Jesus describes his work as fulfilling the Law and the Prophets and affirms their enduring authority. Christians examine later claims in relation to that testimony, rather than simply adopting a later text as the judge of it.

context.text: Read 6–13. Opponents mock the recipient of the Reminder; the response includes God’s promise to preserve it and recalls earlier rejected messengers.

purpose.text: Understand the theological preservation claim before moving to manuscripts and transmission.

examine.text: Identify what is promised. Keep the promise distinct from the historical questions of copying, variants and transmission; those require their own evidence.

connection.text: Confidence in a sacred text matters to conversion, but competing preservation claims need examination. Follow the manuscript study when the conversation turns to historical evidence.

christian.text: Isaiah affirms the endurance of God’s word, and Jesus says his words will not pass away. These state Christian convictions about preservation; manuscript evidence must still be considered on its own terms.

reviews.scope: Twelve comparisons and primary source context
reviews.note: Checked linked Quran passages and Westminster references. Expanded explanations distinguish divine sonship, creation, sin, forgiveness, salvation, revelation and Scripture. Islamic mercy and interpretive differences are acknowledged. No human theological approval is claimed.
